claims.text: Approximately 7 at.% Zr is an optimal concentration in Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx.
Combining approximately 7 at.% Zr with controlled thermomechanical processing and post-stress-relief annealing produces synergistic lattice distortion and grain refinement.
The proposed lattice-distortion and grain-refinement synergy enhances dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning increases mechanical strength while preserving corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Departures from the optimal Zr content or processing conditions cause phase instability or adverse microstructural features that degrade performance.
Larger Zr atoms generate lattice distortion when incorporated into this alloy.
Tailored thermomechanical processing and stress-relief annealing refine the grain structure and alter the dislocation structure.
An adequate Zr concentration provides solid-solution strengthening through lattice-distortion-mediated dislocation pinning without inducing phase separation.
Optimized thermomechanical processing develops a stable dislocation network that further increases yield strength.
The processed microstructure minimizes diffusion paths relevant to corrosion and oxidation.
The combined composition-processing interaction optimizes the trade-off among low density, strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The approximately 7 at.% Zr alloy receiving optimized processing will have higher yield strength than lower-Zr, higher-Zr, or minimally processed comparators.
The approximately 7 at.% Zr alloy receiving optimized processing will have superior ductility relative to the comparator alloys.
The approximately 7 at.% Zr alloy receiving optimized processing will exhibit lower corrosion rates and less pitting in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
The approximately 7 at.% Zr alloy receiving optimized processing will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain and a more stable oxide scale at 1000–1100 °C.
Excessive Zr causes phase separation and terminates the proposed beneficial regime.
Overly aggressive thermomechanical treatment can cause inverse Hall–Petch behavior.
Residual stresses from overly aggressive processing can undermine corrosion and oxidation resistance.
